summary: The xDrive50e M Sport is the only plug-in hybrid in BMW Australia's X5 range, pairing the 3.0-litre turbo straight-six with a 145kW motor and a 25.7kWh usable battery for 360kW/700Nm and 94km of WLTP electric range — more than any other plug-in hybrid in its price bracket, and enough to run a typical Melbourne commute on grid power alone. Reviewers are consistent that this is the X5 to have if you can charge it: the powertrain is the smoothest and the second-most-powerful in the range, the ride is plush, and the 2700kg towing rating matches the diesel exactly. The catch is what happens when the battery is flat — BMW's own WLTP charge-sustaining figure is 9.6-10.5L/100km, worse than the cheaper xDrive40i petrol's claim — and that at $154,900 the car sits above every tax threshold the FBT and LCT rules define, so the concessions that once carried plug-in hybrids are gone.
pros: 94km of WLTP electric range from a 25.7kWh usable pack (29.5kWh gross) — 25 per cent more capacity than the xDrive45e it replaced, and more electric range than the BMW X3 30e's 85km, the Volvo XC90 T8's 69km or the Land Rover Defender P300e's 48km

41g/km combined CO2 is far inside Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car limit, so duty is charged at the flat $8.40 per $200 green rate rather than the $18.00 per $200 tier a petrol X5 over $150,000 pays — worth roughly $7,400 at this price, the largest single duty saving of any car in the dataset

1.9L/100km on the combined cycle clears the Luxury Car Tax fuel-efficient test of 3.5L/100km, so LCT is levied above the $91,661 threshold instead of the $80,809 one — about $3,580 less tax embedded in the list price than an equivalent diesel or petrol X5

360kW and 700Nm makes it the second-most-powerful X5 behind the $177,900 M60i V8 and comfortably quicker than the $143,900 xDrive40i petrol, while its 2700kg braked tow rating is identical to the xDrive30d diesel — the plug-in gives away no capability to the cars it costs more than

11kW three-phase AC charging fills the pack in about two and a half hours, and the five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and not tied to servicing inside the BMW network, with the high-voltage battery separately covered for six years or 100,000km
cons: The 1.9L/100km label collapses the moment the battery is flat: BMW's own WLTP charge-sustaining figure is 9.6-10.5L/100km and Auto Express measured 25.9mpg (about 10.9L/100km) on petrol alone, which is worse than the cheaper xDrive40i petrol's own 9.3L/100km claim — a buyer who cannot charge at home is paying $11,000 more to use more fuel

The battery costs 150 litres of boot — 500L seats-up against 650L in every other X5, and 1720L folded against 1870L — and the plug-in is five seats only with no third-row option, where a seven-seat Volvo XC90 T8 sits $34,000 cheaper at $120,990

Plug-in hybrids lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and at $154,900 the xDrive50e is more than double the $75,000 FBT cap and far above both the $80,809 ordinary and $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT thresholds — the novated-lease arithmetic that used to justify a car like this no longer applies at all

Charging is AC-only at 11kW with no DC fast-charge capability of any kind, so a flat battery is an overnight or a two-and-a-half-hour wallbox stop and cannot be usefully recovered mid-journey — and there is no vehicle-to-load or vehicle-to-home output

This is a run-out car bought at full list: BMW has revealed the fifth-generation X5 with Australian timing locked in, petrol and diesel arriving in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the replacement 50e xDrive — with up to 102km of WLTP range — by mid-2027, which is a hard deadline on this generation's residual value
